"Fume" as a verb has two meanings. One is literal and physical; the other is about emotion. Both are connected by the same core image — something hot releasing itself into the air.
Meaning 1: To release smoke, gas, or vapor

When a substance actively sends out smoke, toxic gas, or strong-smelling vapor, we say it fumes. This meaning is mostly used in scientific, industrial, or technical situations.

The acid fumed dangerously when it came into contact with water.
The paint was fuming so strongly that we had to open all the windows.

Here, "fume" simply describes a physical process — a substance releasing something into the surrounding air.
Meaning 2: To feel or show intense, burning anger

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in everyday English. When a person is fuming, they are experiencing a deep, hot, overwhelming anger — the kind that doesn't cool down quickly. It's the feeling of being so angry that the emotion is practically radiating off you.

Think of a pressure cooker. The heat is building up inside, and steam is straining to escape. That is what fuming feels like — intense, hot anger that is either boiling beneath the surface or being released in bursts of heated words and agitated behavior.

She was fuming when she found out she hadn't been invited.
He fumed about the decision for the rest of the day.
I sat there fuming silently, too angry to even speak.

A few important things to understand about this meaning:

Fuming suggests ongoing anger. You don't fume for just a moment. When someone is fuming, they are stewing — replaying the event, feeling the anger again and again, unable to let it go. It's not a quick flash of temper. It's anger that lingers and burns.

Fuming can be silent or expressed. Sometimes a fuming person says nothing at all — but their body language, their silence, and their clenched jaw say everything. Other times, a fuming person is actively ranting, complaining, and venting. Both are "fuming." The word doesn't specify whether the anger is held in or let out; it just tells you the anger is intense.

Fuming is not mild. This is not the word you use for small frustrations. If someone cuts in front of you in a short queue, you might be annoyed. If your boss publicly humiliates you in front of your colleagues over something that wasn't your fault, you would be fuming.
How "fume" compares to similar words for anger

Understanding where "fume" sits among related words will sharpen your sense of exactly what it means.

Annoyed / irritated sits at the milder end. These describe a low-level frustration over something small. A fuming person is far past this stage.

Angry is the broad, general word. It covers everything from mild displeasure to intense rage. It tells you little about the degree or the quality of the anger.

Fuming tells you the anger is intense and hot. It carries the image of something steaming, something barely contained. It often suggests the anger is just under the surface, though not always hidden.

Seething is the closest word to fuming. The difference is subtle: seething almost always implies the anger is being held tightly under control on the outside, while something dangerous burns within. A seething person looks calm but is anything but. A fuming person is more likely to show their anger — through their expression, their tone, or their words — even if they're not shouting.

Raging is the most explosive end of the spectrum. A raging person has lost control. Fuming still carries a sense of someone trying (even if struggling) to contain themselves.
The connection between the two meanings

The link between "releasing gas" and "intense anger" is not a coincidence. The emotional meaning grew naturally out of the physical one. An angry person was compared to a boiling substance releasing hot steam — and "fume" came to describe both. When you picture someone fuming with anger, you are essentially picturing a human pressure cooker, steam rising, heat building. That image is baked directly into the word.

She was still fuming the next morning. — The anger carried over; she couldn't shake it.

He left the meeting fuming. — He walked out in a state of intense, barely-controlled anger.

The whole team was left fuming over the unfair rule change. — A group of people, all intensely angry about the same thing.

She fumed in silence, staring out the window. — Intense anger expressed through silence and withdrawn behavior.

He fumed at his boss about being passed over for promotion. — He expressed his anger directly and heatedly.

Notice the prepositions: you fume at someone (directed toward a person), about or over something (directed toward a situation), or sometimes just on your own, with no preposition at all.

What makes "fume" such a vivid and useful word is the image it carries. It doesn't just tell you someone is angry — it tells you the quality of that anger. Hot. Building. Hard to contain. Whether it escapes as heated words or stays trapped behind a tight jaw, the internal experience is the same: a burning, simmering intensity that refuses to go out quickly.
